chunks: Basic op-amp circuit analysis. The question: Basic opamp circuit analysis.
An op-amp (operational amplifier) is a chip that amplifies the voltage difference between its two inputs, plus (+) and minus (minus ), by a huge amount.
When you feed part of its output back to the minus, or inverting, input (negative feedback), it adjusts its output until the two inputs are at nearly the same voltage.
The inputs draw almost no current. That lets two resistors set the gain precisely, without depending on the op-amp's own huge gain.
Think of a thermostat. It compares the room temperature to your setting and keeps heating until the difference is zero.
An op-amp does the same with voltage: it keeps changing its output until the difference between its two inputs is almost zero. Whatever output that takes is your answer.
The analogy fails if the target is out of reach. The op-amp's output can't go beyond its supply rails.
The inverting node sits at 0 volts (virtual ground), so I in = V in/R 1 and it must all flow through R f. Gain = -R f/R 1 = -10; input resistance is R 1 = 1 kilohms.
Negative feedback: sending the output back to the inverting input so errors get corrected. Virtual ground: an input held at 0 volts by feedback without being connected to ground.
Gain: output voltage divided by input voltage. Rails: the supply voltages, which are the limits of the output. KCL: the currents into a node sum to zero.
Build an inverting amplifier with R1 = 1 kilohms in and Rf = 10 kilohms in feedback, with the plus input grounded. Apply 0. 5 volts.
Feedback holds the minus input at 0 volts (a virtual ground), so 0. 5 milliamps flows through R1. None enters the op-amp, so all of it goes through Rf and drops 0.
5 milliamps times 10 kilohms equals 5 volts. The output is minus 5 volts , a gain of minus 10. That is the whole idea.
"First check for negative feedback. If it's there, the op-amp holds both inputs at the same voltage and they draw no current, so I just do KCL at the inverting node.
For an inverting amp the input current Vin over R1 flows through Rf, so gain is minus Rf over R1.
For a non-inverting amp the feedback divider sets the inverting node equal to Vin, so gain is one plus Rf over R1. Same method for summing amps and integrators.
Then I'd check real limits: rails, gain-bandwidth, and slew rate."
